title: Declaration of Interdependence
author: Sylvia Duarte
summary: A conference report from the National Hybrid Schools Conference, drawing together school founders, administrators, and parents from nearly every state. Despite wildly divergent values — classical educators, culturally responsive schools, microschools for neurodiverse students — the room shared one conviction: children deserve better than what current schooling provides. Gerard Robinson framed the movement not as a declaration of independence from failing systems, but a 'declaration of interdependence' — people across ideological lines uniting around the value of learning.
points: The National Hybrid Schools Conference drew founders, parents, PhDs, and policymakers representing schools from 10-student microschools to multi-campus hybrid programs.
Keynote speaker Coi Marie Morefield: 'This is the most ideologically diverse room I have ever been in as an educator' — but united by one conviction that children deserve better.

Gerard Robinson: this isn't just independence from failing systems, it's interdependence — people who eat different food, come from different zip codes, voted differently, united on one thing: learning matters.
Robinson on institutional pushback: 'The opposite of love, biblically speaking, isn't hate — it's fear. And what you represent to them is fear.'
Practical sessions covered profit-and-loss, surviving regulatory scrutiny, AI-powered classrooms, project-based learning, and neurodiversity as innovation driver.

Dr. Richelle Brooks — once a teenage mother, briefly homeless — runs a public charter for high school dropouts being shut down; pivoting to three microschools using 501(c)(3) structure and grant/church funding.

Tocqueville's observation about Americans forming associations rather than waiting for state direction applies directly: these founders are rolling up their sleeves and raising institutions their communities need.
quotes: Call this a declaration of interdependence. You have people in this room who eat different food, come from different zip codes, voted for different people, read different books — but you come together on one thing. Learning matters. —Gerard Robinson
I want to encourage you to remain unpopular. Fifty years from now, someone will look back and wonder what took so long. So keep up the revolution. —Gerard Robinson
